articles.title: AI Incidents Expose Your Team's Oversight Blind Spot
articles.excerpt: The Decision Nobody Can Verify Your AI agent just made a call during a production outage. It rerouted traffic, suppressed an alert, or escalated a ticket. In 2026, that scenario is no longer hypotheti…
articles.body: The Decision Nobody Can Verify Your AI agent just made a call during a production outage. It rerouted traffic, suppressed an alert, or escalated a ticket. In 2026, that scenario is no longer hypothetical for most mid-to-large engineering organizations. The uncomfortable question is this: can anyone on your team actually reconstruct what the system decided, why it decided it, and whether that decision made things better or worse? Most teams answer that question with silence. Not because they lack smart people, but because the people who understand the cloud infrastructure and the people who understand the AI stack are sitting in different rooms, reading different dashboards, and operating under different incident commanders. That structural gap is where failures hide.

articles.body: Originally published on tamiz.pro . MongoDB's aggregation framework is powerful enough to replace entire ETL pipelines, but at scale it becomes a performance minefield. A pipeline that processes 10,000 documents in milliseconds can grind a replica set to a halt when fed 100 million. articles.title: Three documents that keep my AI coding agent honest (free templates + Claude Code skill)
articles.excerpt: I run a one-person R&D operation that ships industrial sensing products — analogue boards, microcontroller firmware, PC tools. Most of the typing is done by AI coding agents (mainly Claude Code). They…
articles.body: I run a one-person R&D operation that ships industrial sensing products — analogue boards, microcontroller firmware, PC tools. Most of the typing is done by AI coding agents (mainly Claude Code). They are fast, and for a year they failed in the same four ways: They extended the scope without asking. They reported "done" without running the test. They stated facts they had not checked ("the sibling project uses the same part"). They repeated the same mistake in the next session. None of this was fixed by a better model. It was fixed by a process the agent cannot skip. I've generalized it into a small kit and put it on GitHub under MIT: ai-rd-process-kit .

articles.title: TypeScript Tuples in 2026: Labeled Elements, Variadic Spreads, and When a Tuple Beats an Interface
articles.excerpt: TypeScript Tuples in 2026: Labeled Elements, Variadic Spreads, and When a Tuple Beats an Interface This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review. Most TypeScri…
articles.body: TypeScript Tuples in 2026: Labeled Elements, Variadic Spreads, and When a Tuple Beats an Interface This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review. Most TypeScript engineers reach for interfaces when they need structured data. That reflex breaks when an API returns coordinates, a useState hook returns [value, setter] , or middleware needs to compose through a chain of handlers. Arrays do not enforce length or per-index types. Interfaces force named property access when destructuring is cleaner. The type system accepts [string, number] as valid but offers no hints at the call site. Engineers write result[0] with no indication whether zero holds a user ID or an error message. The compiler stays silent when position assumptions drift.

articles.body: TL;DR A new SIM Manager connector for Gemini has appeared on a Pixel 9 running the Android 17 QPR3 beta, likely by accident. It lets Gemini set up a new eSIM, convert a physical SIM to an eSIM, transfer profiles, restore them from a backup, and delete them. The connector’s details page also shows the rules Gemini follows, including several things it won’t do, like turning on an eSIM you’ve already installed. Gemini can already work with a long list of apps on your phone, from Gmail to YouTube Music. articles.title: How 'spacewalking' underwater made me feel like I was really in space
articles.excerpt: Analog Astronaut Commander and Aquanaut Michaela Musilova led underwater simulated “spacewalks” in low visibility to test astronaut safety and communication protocols during simulated space missions.
articles.body: I was breathing just fine through my life support systems, but I kept feeling an urge to double check that everything was ok with my "spacesuit" before heading out on this "spacewalk." I have worn many different types of spacesuits on Earth during my career, but for the first time in my life, I knew that I couldn’t just stop to breathe the air outside if there were an emergency. That's because I was underwater. On this excursion, I was leading a simulated space mission underwater called SEA STAR. My " spacesuit " was actually scuba diving gear, and the simulated spacewalks , or EVAs (Extra-Vehicular Activities), included outings where we explored underwater environments.

articles.excerpt: The four volunteers who lived and worked in a simulated NASA Mars mission for more than a year will exit their habitat on Saturday, Oct. 31, after 378 days of isolation in a facility at the agency’s J…
articles.body: Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) Mission 2 crew members (from left) Ross Elder, Matthew Montgomery, Ellen Ellis, and James Spicer, pose for a photo on Oct. 8, 2025. Credit: NASA The four volunteers who lived and worked in a simulated NASA Mars mission for more than a year will exit their habitat on Saturday, Oct. 31, after 378 days of isolation in a facility at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. Health and performance data collected from the simulation can help NASA develop methods to counter human spaceflight risks for future Artemis and Moon Base missions. Beginning at 3 p.m. EDT, NASA will provide live coverage of the volunteers’ departure from the Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA, pronounced cha-pea’-ah) mission habitat.
